question: How do we measure and interpret the relationship between two variables (correlation, least squares fit, R-squared) and what evidence can support causation?

results.claim: Pearson correlation is bounded between -1 and +1.
results.setup: Definition of rho as mean product of standard scores; proof via Cauchy-Schwarz
results.quote: Also, the result is necessarily between −1 and +1.

results.claim: R-squared equals the squared Pearson correlation for a linear least squares model.
R2 = 0.64 means the model reduces the MSE of predictions by 64% (explains 64% of variability).
results.quote: If a model yields R2 = 0.64, you could say that the model explains 64% of the variability, or it might be more precise to say that it reduces the MSE of your predictions by 64%.

results.claim: Pearson correlation only measures linear relationships; a nonlinear dependence can give rho=0.
results.quote: Pearson’s correlation only measures linear relationships.

results.claim: Pearson is not robust to outliers; Anscombe's quartet has four data sets with the same correlation.
results.quote: Anscombe’s quartet demonstrates this effect; it contains four data sets with the same correlation.

results.claim: Randomised controlled trial is the most reliable way to demonstrate causation.
results.quote: A randomized controlled trial is the most reliable way to demonstrate a causal relationship

limits: Only simple (one explanatory variable) linear regression; multivariate regression is explicitly left out ('that's a whole other book').
Covers no inference on correlation (no confidence intervals or p-values for rho, beta or R2).
Printed rho formula in terms of deviations (sum dx dy / (sum dx sum dy)) is wrong as typeset; correct form is sum dx dy / sqrt(sum dx^2 sum dy^2), or Cov/(sigma_X sigma_Y).
No numeric results for BRFSS correlation, slope or R2 are printed; they are left as exercises.
Rank handling: ties get arbitrary ranks in the simple solution; chapter says averaged ranks are strictly correct.
Book is dated (pyplot code, Python 2 era, thinkstats.com links, R via Python).
practices: Always look at a scatterplot before computing a correlation coefficient (p.110).
Use standard scores for Pearson, and percentile ranks (Spearman) when data are skewed or have outliers (p.108, 114).
Alternatively transform to near-normal (e.g. log of lognormal data) then use Pearson (p.114).
Jitter only for visualisation, never for analysis (p.113).
Use alpha transparency for moderate data, hexbin for large data; hexbin hides outliers (p.113).
Consider whether squared residuals are the right loss; a cost function may be more appropriate (p.116).
To support causation use time ordering, randomisation (RCT), natural experiments, or regression/stratification controls (p.119-120).
Control for a confounder by stratifying, e.g. compare first vs other babies within mother's-age groups (p.120).
